findings.element: b.css @media (min-width: 1024px) → [data-medium="full"] .b-ownerField { height: 100dvh; display: flex; overflow: hidden }, nested inside shell.css .tl-page { padding: var(--stage-pad) } plus .tl-caption
findings.problem: The round's headline structural claim — "the page does not scroll at 1024 and above ... the lock's 'the horizon never moves at desk width', built properly" — is not what the file does. The frame is declared 100dvh but it sits inside .tl-page, which adds 40px of --stage-pad top and bottom plus the .tl-caption line, so the document is one viewport PLUS 107px. Driven at 1024, 1152, 1279, 1280 and 1440 (at both 800 and 960 tall) the window scroll range is 107px at every single one, and scrolling it moves .b-num from y=268 to y=161 — the horizon travels the full 107px. This is the same defect the file records as fixed ("sticky alone let the rail drift 191px before it stuck"), a smaller number wearing a new mechanism, and it is the round-8 stylesheet-order case repeating: a fix recorded as done that the composition around it makes inert. Nothing in interaction-check.mjs measures window scroll range at desk width, so 605 assertions pass over it.
findings.fix: Make the page the frame, not just the field. In b.css's @media (min-width: 1024px) block, change the existing rule to `[data-medium="full"] .b-ownerField { height: auto; flex: 1 1 auto; min-height: 0; display: flex; flex-direction: column; overflow: hidden; }` and add above it `[data-medium="full"] .tl-page:has(.b-ownerField) { height: 100dvh; padding-bottom: 0; overflow: hidden; }` and `[data-medium="full"] .tl-stage:has(.b-ownerField) { display: flex; flex-direction: column; flex: 1 1 auto; min-height: 0; }`. Verified live in Playwright: window scroll range goes 107 → 0 at 1440x960, the plan pane still scrolls its own content, the foot lands at y=868 and the first moment at y=570 — the composition is untouched. Then assert `documentElement.scrollHeight - clientHeight === 0` for the owner states at 1024/1152/1279/1280/1440.

findings.element: render-b.js place() — `var gap = el.getAttribute("data-stack") === "follow" ? 1 : 10;` and `var height = copy.getBoundingClientRect().height;`, against b.css `.b-item[data-stack="lead"] .b-copy { padding-bottom: var(--gap-snug) }`
findings.problem: closeRun() is the only writer of data-stack and it runs after a row has already been measured, so the render that CREATES a stacked pair measures the leader before the 12px padding-bottom that data-stack="lead" is about to give it. Driven through the gate's own scenario (owner-editing, one press of −7, 1440x960): the follower lands at --push 90px, its .b-copy top at 660 against the leader's bottom at 661 — the two rows overlap by 1px, the follower's hairline border-top sitting inside the leader's padding. Then the next layout pass with no data change at all — one pixel of window resize, document.fonts.ready, opening the editor, the next stepper press — recomputes it to 102px and the row snaps down 12px. Under prefers-reduced-motion it teleports, because this is a re-layout, not the declared transition. The gate is built so it cannot see this: collisions() explicitly filters out `data-stack === "follow"`, and the six stacked-pair assertions compare attributes, tops, marks and counts — never the one piece of geometry that is wrong.
findings.fix: Group before measuring. In place(), insert a first pass over the sorted `items` that writes data-stack and the .b-unitSaid sentence for every run — walk the array, compare data-away with the previous row, set "" / "lead" / "follow" and the "first/then of N moments on this day" string — then run the existing placement loop, which now reads a data-stack that is already true for this render. Delete `run`, `closeRun()` and its trailing call from the measuring loop. Add an assertion that measures the real gap between a lead .b-copy's bottom and its follower's top (expect 11px, not −1) and re-measures it after a 1px resize.

findings.element: b.css `.b-seg { display: inline-flex; border: 1px solid var(--fore-28); border-radius: 6px; overflow: hidden; }` and its two `.b-seg button` children, against shell.css `:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--focus); outline-offset: 2px }`
findings.problem: The Shown/Hidden buttons fill the plate edge to edge (measured at 1440: plate 310x39, buttons at 1,1,70,37 and 71,1,72,37), so a 2px outline drawn 2px outside each button's border box falls entirely inside the parent's overflow:hidden clip and is never painted. Tabbed to with the keyboard, both controls take focus with no visible treatment at all — proven by screenshotting the focused "Hidden" button, then setting .b-seg overflow to visible and screenshotting again: the white ring appears only in the second. That is a WCAG 2.4.7 failure on two consecutive tab stops, and they are the two controls that decide what a guest sees, on a panel whose own comment claims "the keyboard gets exactly what the pointer gets, which it did not". The gate's "focus paints a visible treatment" is the passing assertion that proves nothing: it focuses `document.querySelector("button, a[href], [tabindex], input")` — one element, the bar's first .b-act, in a different state — and asserts only that computed outline-width is above zero, which is equally true of a ring that is clipped away.
findings.fix: Drop `overflow: hidden` from `.b-seg` and put the corner clip on the children: `.b-seg button:first-child { border-radius: 5px 0 0 5px }` and `.b-seg button:last-child { border-radius: 0 5px 5px 0 }`. Verified: the 2px ring then paints on both buttons on both grounds with no change to the plate's shape. Then replace the gate's single-element check with a loop over every visible focusable element in every state that screenshots the element before and after focus and fails on an identical image — a clipped ring, or a ring the same colour as the fill it sits on, both fail.

findings.element: render-b.js `states["owner-draft"]` — `var was = F.publication, wasLabel = F.updatedLabel; ... var node = ownerSurface({}); F.publication = was; F.updatedLabel = wasLabel; return node;`
findings.problem: The fourteenth state exists, per the round note, so the draft branch is finally rendered — but it hands the record back before anyone can press anything, so the state is only true until it is touched. Driven: owner-draft correctly shows "Only you can see this", the verb "Publish" and "Updated 16 July 2026"; pressing that Publish calls go("publish"), which re-reads the restored record and renders the headline "Mara & Finn have had this since 15 July." with the strap "The link is below." Two screens one press apart contradict each other about whether the couple are already holding the plan — on the surface where the owner is closest to giving it away, and it is the self-contradicting-facts class this file has already paid for twice. The consequence for the panel is that the publish screen's draft half — the "Send it to Mara & Finn." headline and the "Ready to send. The link is below." strap — is rendered by no graded state, appears in none of the fourteen frames, and has never been through audit.mjs.
findings.fix: Stop restoring. In `states["owner-draft"]`, set `F.publication = { state: "draft", publishedAt: null }` and `F.updatedLabel = F.fmt.medium(F.today) + " " + F.fmt.year(F.today)` and leave them set for the session, exactly as the `add` and `setday` handlers already do; delete the `was`/`wasLabel` save-and-restore. The existing data-act="copy" handler does the rest — it already flips publication to published and repaints — so "taking the link publishes it" becomes true from this state too. Add owner-draft → Publish to the shot list so the draft publish screen enters the measured perimeter.

findings.element: render-b.js wireOwner, the `add` branch — `id: "moment-" + (F.milestones.length + 1)`, against `recordFor(id)` which returns `F.milestones.filter(m => m.id === id)[0]`
findings.problem: The id is minted from the array's current length, and the array shrinks on every delete and on every undo of an add, so the counter runs backwards and reissues ids that are still in use. Driven at 1440: Add, Add, delete the first of the two, Add — the fixture now holds two records with id "moment-12". recordFor() returns the first, so the editor opened on the NEW moment writes to the OLD one: typing "Rehearsal dinner" into the new moment's title field left the records reading ["Rehearsal dinner@2026-07-18", "@2026-07-17"] while the two rows on screen read ["Rehearsal dinner", "Untitled moment"] — the visible row and the record it claims to be are different moments, and they swap over on the next remount. setAway() and setVisibility() resolve through the same accessor, so a date press and a Hidden toggle land on the wrong moment the same way. No console error, no gate assertion, and audit.mjs only ever sees the first render.
findings.fix: Mint monotonically instead of from the length. Add a module-scoped `var minted = F.milestones.length;` beside `var history = [];` in render-b.js and use `id: "moment-" + (++minted)` in the add branch. Nothing else changes: the counter never goes backwards, so no id is ever reissued, and it cannot collide with the fixture's demo-audience-item-* ids. Add an assertion that after add/add/delete/add the set of milestone ids contains no duplicates.

biggestWin: The measure is the real thing, and it holds up under driving. One writer — setAway() — computes the date, and every other fact on the screen is derived from it in the same frame, so the count, the date line, the row's accessible name, the stepper readout, the date field and the gap sentence cannot drift apart; twenty presses in a row leave the ladder strictly proportional and the ceiling states itself rather than swallowing the press. Around it sits a reversibility model most shipped products do not have: one surface that travels to wherever the change was made, every entry carrying its own undo closure, and place-keeping that restores the window scroll, the pane scroll AND the exact control that made the change, across delete, rename, hide and move. That is Linear-grade mechanism rather than a picture of one, and it is the part of this the rest of the suite should inherit first.
